stem: A research coordinator built on the Agent SDK runs web search and document analysis subagents, then delegates to a synthesis subagent that has its own system prompt and a read-only tool set. By that point the coordinator's history holds about 150k tokens of raw search output. Synthesis drafts keep missing findings that the analysis subagent reported. What is the best way to get those findings to synthesis while keeping it focused and within its tool restrictions?

options.text: Give the synthesis subagent the web search and document tools as well, so it can re-retrieve whatever finding it notices is missing while drafting the report.
Turn on fork mode and have the coordinator spawn synthesis as a fork, so it inherits the full conversation, including every finding, without restating anything.
Pass the complete findings from the search and analysis subagents in the synthesis subagent's delegation prompt, each with its source metadata attached.
Have the coordinator record the key findings in auto memory as they arrive, so that every subagent spawned later in the session loads them at startup.

explanation: A non-fork subagent starts with a fresh, isolated context: its own system prompt, the delegation message and project instructions, but not the coordinator's history. Findings from earlier subagents therefore have to be written into the delegation prompt. Doing so keeps synthesis on its own definition and tools, and gives it only the distilled findings instead of 150k tokens of raw output.

distractorNotes.a: Re-retrieval duplicates work the other subagents already did, and handing synthesis search tools breaks the read-only restriction the scenario asks to keep. The findings already exist; they just have to be passed.
distractorNotes.b: A fork does inherit the whole conversation, but it also runs with the parent's system prompt, tools and model instead of the synthesis definition, and it carries all 150k tokens of raw output. That gives up both the focus and the tool restriction.
distractorNotes.d: The main conversation's auto memory is explicitly not loaded into non-fork subagents, so nothing recorded there would reach synthesis.

sourceNote: Subagents § Manage subagent context (auto memory not loaded) and § How forks differ from other subagents

stem: An engineer implements an autonomous customer support agent loop using the Messages API. The loop intermittently terminates prematurely or runs into runaway execution. How should the control flow determine whether to execute requested tools or return the final response?

options.text: Inspect the response stop_reason: continue the execution loop when it is 'tool_use', and terminate the loop when it is 'end_turn'.
Parse the raw assistant text blocks for natural language completion markers such as 'FINAL_ANSWER' before evaluating tool use content blocks.
Inspect the assistant message blocks for text content, exiting the loop immediately whenever any non-empty conversational text precedes tool calls.
Rely strictly on a fixed client counter capping execution at five turns, forcing loop termination when the counter threshold is reached.

explanation: In standard agentic loops with the Messages API, the canonical control flow checks stop_reason on each turn. A stop_reason of 'tool_use' indicates that Claude has generated tool call requests and is awaiting tool_result blocks. A stop_reason of 'end_turn' indicates Claude has concluded its turn and provided its final response. Relying on text parsing, presence of conversational text, or arbitrary iteration caps leads to premature termination or uncontrolled execution.

distractorNotes.b: Natural language markers in text are probabilistic, brittle, and not part of the API contract for loop termination.
distractorNotes.c: Claude frequently provides explanatory text alongside tool_use content blocks; presence of text does not imply completion.
distractorNotes.d: Hard iteration caps are safety backstops against infinite loops, not the primary mechanism for normal workflow termination.

sourceNote: Handling stop reasons tool_use and end_turn to control agentic loop lifecycles

stem: An agent generates a tool_use block requesting customer order details. What is the required structure for passing the backend database response back into the conversation for the next model turn?

options.text: Overwrite the initial system prompt with a JSON payload containing the retrieved order data before dispatching the next conversational turn.
Send a user message containing a tool_result content block referencing the matching tool_use_id from the assistant message.
Append a simulated assistant message containing the retrieved order JSON formatted inside markdown code fences to represent the tool output.
Send a new user message containing the order JSON as plain text, without a tool_result block or the tool_use_id.

explanation: When Claude requests a tool call, the caller must respond with a message having role: 'user' containing a content block of type 'tool_result' that specifies tool_use_id matching the id of the tool_use block. This maintains the conversational turn structure required by the Messages API so Claude can reason over the result in subsequent turns.

distractorNotes.a: The system prompt provides static instructions; mutating it with dynamic tool outputs degrades prompt caching and violates API patterns.
distractorNotes.c: Tool outputs must be provided in user messages with type 'tool_result', not as fabricated assistant messages.
distractorNotes.d: Plain text in a user message does not satisfy the pending tool_use and leaves the tool call unresolved; the API requires a tool_result block referencing the matching tool_use_id.

sourceNote: Returning tool_result content blocks in user messages paired with tool_use_id

stem: An architect is designing an incident investigation agent. Post-mortems show that about a third of past incidents were failure modes the runbook did not describe, and that the useful next query usually depended on what the previous one revealed. The on-call team wants the agent to reach a root cause without running every diagnostic on every incident. Which design fits best?

options.text: A decision tree with one branch per runbook failure category and a fallback branch that escalates to a human whenever the observed symptoms match no known category.
A model-driven agentic loop in which Claude chooses each next diagnostic tool from the observations gathered so far, and the loop ends on its own when Claude stops calling tools.
A fixed pipeline that runs the full diagnostic query set in parallel at the start of every incident, then hands all of the output to Claude in a single analysis call.
A fixed prompt chain that walks the runbook steps in order, with Claude summarizing each step's output before the chain moves on to the next predefined query.

explanation: Model-driven decision-making, where Claude reasons about which tool to call next from what it has observed, is the pattern the guide sets against pre-configured decision trees and tool sequences. It suits open-ended investigation. Here a third of incidents are unscripted, each query depends on the last one's result, and the team wants to avoid exhaustive querying, so all three conditions favour an adaptive loop.

distractorNotes.a: The tree handles known categories well, but a third of incidents would fall through to the escalation branch without any investigation, which misses the goal for exactly the incidents that need adaptive reasoning.
distractorNotes.c: Querying everything up front is deterministic and simple, but it is the exhaustive querying the team wants to avoid, and later queries cannot be shaped by what earlier ones found.
distractorNotes.d: A prompt chain suits predictable, repeatable sequences. Walking fixed runbook steps cannot follow evidence into a failure mode the runbook does not describe.

sourceNote: Exam Guide v1.0 § Task Statements 1.1, 1.6 — model-driven tool choice vs pre-configured sequences for open-ended investigation

stem: During an agentic workflow, an API call returns stop_reason: 'max_tokens' while generating arguments for a database write tool. What is the proper recovery handling in the orchestration layer?

options.text: Discard the incomplete tool_use block without executing it, then retry the request with a higher max_tokens value so the full tool call is generated.
Append the truncated assistant content to the history and send a user turn asking Claude to continue where it left off, so the rest of the arguments get generated.
Retry the identical request unchanged, on the assumption that the max_tokens cutoff was a transient glitch that is unlikely to recur on the next attempt.
Execute the partial tool call with the arguments that did arrive, then send the tool result back so Claude can notice any missing fields and correct them itself.

explanation: When a response stops on max_tokens with an incomplete tool_use block, the documented recovery is to retry the request with a higher max_tokens value to get the full tool use. A truncated block is not a valid call, so it must not be executed.

distractorNotes.b: Continuing from where the response left off is the documented pattern for truncated text. An incomplete tool_use block cannot be completed that way; the documented fix is a retry with a higher max_tokens value.
distractorNotes.c: The cutoff is deterministic: the same request with the same limit will be truncated again. The limit has to be raised.
distractorNotes.d: Running a database write with truncated arguments risks committing corrupted data before anything can correct it. An incomplete tool_use block must never be executed.

sourceNote: Detecting and recovering from max_tokens stop reason during tool execution

stem: In a four-subagent research system, the team lets the document analysis subagent message the synthesis subagent directly instead of returning through the coordinator, to save a round trip. Since then, when document analysis fails partway, synthesis sometimes drafts from partial data, and the coordinator's logs hold no record of the failure. What is the best fix?

options.text: Keep the direct channel, but have both subagents write every message they exchange to a shared log that the coordinator reads before accepting the final report.
Merge document analysis and synthesis into a single subagent, so there is no handoff between them for a partial failure to slip through unnoticed.
Move both subagents into an agent team, where teammates share a task list and message each other directly, so failures surface through task status.
Route all subagent results back through the coordinator, which sees each failure, decides how to recover and controls what information reaches synthesis.

explanation: In a hub-and-spoke design, the coordinator manages all communication between subagents, error handling and information routing. Routing everything through it restores the observability, consistent error handling and controlled information flow that the direct channel bypassed. The coordinator can then retry, re-delegate, or tell synthesis that its input is partial.

distractorNotes.a: A shared log adds after-the-fact visibility, but synthesis still acts on partial data before the coordinator can intervene. Error handling stays spread across two subagents instead of being centralized.
distractorNotes.b: Merging removes the handoff but gives up the separation of concerns and context isolation the specialized subagents provide. The real defect is that the failure bypassed the coordinator.
distractorNotes.c: Agent teams are built around direct peer messaging and self-coordination, which is the pattern that caused the problem here. They also add coordination overhead and token cost.

sourceNote: Exam Guide v1.0 § Task Statement 1.2 — route subagent communication via the coordinator for observability and consistent error handling

stem: A multi-agent research pipeline is tasked with analyzing 'Emerging Trends in Global Clean Energy'. Each subagent completes successfully, but the final output covers only solar photovoltaics, completely omitting wind, geothermal, nuclear, and grid storage. Logs indicate subagents answered their assigned prompts faithfully. What is the root cause?

options.text: The web search subagent exceeded its token context window and silently truncated non-solar search results before coordinator retrieval.
The coordinator agent decomposed the topic too narrowly into solar-specific subtasks, failing to partition the full research scope.
The document analysis subagent applied an overly aggressive relevance filter that rejected non-solar whitepapers during preprocessing.
The synthesis subagent lacks few-shot examples demonstrating how to merge disparate renewable energy technologies into cohesive reports.

explanation: The exam guide names overly narrow task decomposition by the coordinator as a risk that leads to incomplete coverage of broad research topics. When subagents execute their assigned tasks faithfully but the output omits whole sectors, the failure is in what the coordinator assigned: decomposing 'Global Clean Energy' into only solar subtasks means only solar gets researched.

distractorNotes.a: Logs showed subagents answered their assigned prompts faithfully; token truncation would produce incomplete or error responses.
distractorNotes.c: The problem lies in what tasks were assigned, not in the filtering of valid assigned topics.
distractorNotes.d: Synthesis agents cannot combine information that upstream agents were never assigned to collect.

sourceNote: Exam Guide v1.0 § Task Statement 1.2 — overly narrow coordinator decomposition leads to incomplete coverage of broad topics

stem: An enterprise research assistant sends every request through all four subagents: search, document analysis, quantitative analysis and synthesis. Most traffic is quick policy lookups such as the travel per diem, which take 40 seconds and cost as much as a competitive analysis. The team wants to cut cost and latency on simple requests without hurting the deep ones. What is the most effective change?

options.text: Train a separate classifier on historical requests to label each one simple or complex before the coordinator runs, and send only the complex ones to the pipeline.
Have the coordinator assess each request and pick the subagents it needs, answering simple lookups with a direct tool call and keeping the full pipeline for research.
Send each request to the search subagent first, and fan out to the other three when search reports a self-assessed confidence below a set threshold.
Keep the full pipeline for every request, but run the four subagents in parallel instead of in sequence, so simple lookups finish faster at the same token cost.

explanation: Deciding which subagents to invoke based on query complexity is part of the coordinator's job, instead of always routing through the full pipeline. It addresses the cost and the latency of simple requests at the point where the decision already happens, and it needs no new infrastructure.

distractorNotes.a: A trained classifier could work, but it adds labelled data, a model to maintain and an extra hop in front of a coordinator that can already judge complexity. That is over-engineered for a first fix.
distractorNotes.c: Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated, so a subagent that is wrong but confident would skip the analysis a complex request needs.
distractorNotes.d: Parallelism cuts latency, but every lookup still pays for four subagents, so the cost problem stays. The dependent stages, such as synthesis, also cannot run in parallel with their inputs.

sourceNote: Exam Guide v1.0 § Task Statement 1.2 — coordinator selects subagents by query complexity, not always the full pipeline

stem: A multi-agent research pipeline produces a synthesis draft that explicitly notes it could not find data on regulatory approval timelines in Japan, though the underlying sources for that topic do exist and were simply never retrieved. The coordinator still holds the search subagent and the original findings in context. How should the coordinator best close this gap?

options.text: Re-delegate only a targeted query for the Japanese approval timelines to the search subagent, then hand the new findings back to synthesis for an updated draft.
Give the synthesis subagent the web search tools as well, so it can fill any coverage gap it notices itself without another round trip through the coordinator.
Accept the draft as final and add an explicit 'data unavailable for Japan' limitation note, so the gap is disclosed openly to the reader instead of silently hidden.
Re-run the full pipeline with a broader decomposition that names Japan explicitly, so every subagent re-covers the topic with the missing region in its scope.

explanation: This is the iterative refinement loop the coordinator owns: evaluate synthesis output for gaps, re-delegate to search with a targeted query, then re-invoke synthesis. The coordinator still holds the search subagent and the other findings, and those findings are sound, so only the missing slice needs new work.

distractorNotes.b: A narrowly scoped lookup tool on synthesis can suit simple fact checks. Filling a whole missing topic is a research task, though, and giving synthesis the full search tool set over-provisions it and bypasses the coordinator's control of the loop.
distractorNotes.c: Disclosing a gap is right when the data genuinely does not exist. Here the sources exist and were never retrieved, so labelling the gap as unavailable misreports it.
distractorNotes.d: A full re-run repeats every sound piece of work to fix one missing slice, at the cost of a whole extra pipeline run.

sourceNote: Exam Guide v1.0 § Task Statement 1.2 — iterative refinement: find gaps, re-delegate targeted queries, re-invoke synthesis

stem: A coordinator sends three parallel web search subagents the same prompt about autonomous vehicle safety. The report must cover regulatory frameworks, crash incident data and sensor hardware reliability. Logs show the three subagents returned largely the same top-ranked articles. What change best cuts the duplicate retrieval while keeping the three searches in parallel?

options.text: Keep the identical prompts, raise each subagent's result count so the long tail differs, and deduplicate the merged hits with a post-processing step before synthesis.
Give each subagent a distinct persona in its system prompt, such as regulator, engineer and journalist, and let each choose its own queries from that perspective.
Run the subagents one after another, passing each one the articles already found and telling it to find different ones, so no article is fetched twice.
Assign each subagent one of the report's distinct dimensions, regulation, crash data or sensor reliability, so the three search scopes do not overlap.

explanation: Partitioning the research scope, for example by giving each subagent a distinct subtopic, is how a coordinator avoids duplicated work. The report's three dimensions give a natural non-overlapping split, and the subagents still run in parallel.

distractorNotes.a: Deduplication hides the symptom after the tokens have been spent. The subagents still retrieve the same articles, which is the waste.
distractorNotes.b: Personas change tone and emphasis but do not bound scope. Three perspectives on the same broad topic still converge on the same top-ranked articles.
distractorNotes.c: Sequencing removes duplicates but gives up the parallelism the scenario asks to keep, adding the full latency of each search.

sourceNote: Exam Guide v1.0 § Task Statement 1.2 — partition research scope by distinct subtopics or source types to minimize duplication

stem: When configuring a coordinator agent using the Claude Agent SDK, what configuration is mandatory to allow the coordinator to spawn subagents?

options.text: The coordinator must embed each subagent's full system prompt inside its own system prompt, since the SDK cannot load subagent definitions separately.
The coordinator's allowedTools configuration must explicitly include the 'Task' tool.
The coordinator must set a maxSubagents concurrency limit in its options, or the SDK refuses to spawn any subagent at all.
The coordinator must declare a shared SQLite database connection string in its environment to coordinate state across processes.

explanation: The exam guide names the Task tool as the mechanism for spawning subagents and states that allowedTools must include "Task" for a coordinator to invoke subagents. Subagent definitions are supplied separately through AgentDefinition configuration, so none of the other options is a prerequisite.

distractorNotes.a: Subagents are declared through AgentDefinition configuration (descriptions, system prompts, tool restrictions), not by inlining their prompts into the coordinator; the stated requirement is 'Task' in allowedTools.
distractorNotes.c: No concurrency-limit option gates spawning; the requirement the guide states is that allowedTools include 'Task'.
distractorNotes.d: Subagents need no shared database; the coordinator passes the context each subagent needs explicitly in its delegation prompt.

sourceNote: Exam Guide v1.0 § Task Statement 1.3 — Task tool spawns subagents; allowedTools must include "Task" for a coordinator

stem: An Agent SDK coordinator reviews pull requests with three specialized subagents: security scanning, dependency auditing and lint checking. Each subagent has its own restricted tool set, and the three checks are independent of each other. Reviews currently take three coordinator turns because the subagents run one at a time. What is the best way to cut the latency without giving up the tool restrictions?

options.text: Combine the three checks into one subagent with the union of their tool sets, so a single delegation covers the whole review in one coordinator turn.
Have the coordinator emit all three Task tool calls in a single response, so the three subagents run in parallel, each with its own definition.
Turn on fork mode and have the coordinator fork three times, so each check starts with the coordinator's full analysis of the pull request already in context.
Keep one Task call per turn, but pass each subagent the previous subagent's results so the later checks can skip anything already covered.

explanation: A coordinator spawns parallel subagents by emitting multiple Task tool calls in one response instead of across separate turns. Each call launches a subagent from its own definition, with its own system prompt and tool restrictions, and because the checks are independent, none has to wait for another.

distractorNotes.a: One subagent does cut the delegations to one, but it runs the checks sequentially and gives up the per-check tool restrictions the scenario asks to keep.
distractorNotes.c: A fork runs with the parent's system prompt and tools rather than a specialized definition, which gives up the restrictions. Fork mode is also off by default in the Agent SDK.
distractorNotes.d: Chaining suits dependent steps. These checks are independent, so passing results along adds nothing and keeps the three-turn latency.

sourceNote: Exam Guide v1.0 § Task Statement 1.3 — parallel subagents via multiple Task tool calls in a single coordinator response

stem: A document analysis subagent extracts findings from 40 clinical trial reports and passes them to a synthesis subagent that writes a cited literature review. Reviewers find claims attributed to the wrong trial, mostly where synthesis combined findings from several reports. How should the handoff format change to preserve attribution without making synthesis re-read the reports?

options.text: Write each finding to a shared database and pass synthesis only the row IDs, so it looks up the text and citation of each finding when it needs them.
Keep the narrative summary but add an inline citation such as (Trial 12, p. 4) after each sentence, so that every claim carries its source reference in the prose.
Pass each finding as a structured record that separates the claim itself from its metadata: source document, trial identifier, URL and page number.
Group the findings by topic and add a numbered source list at the end, so synthesis can match each topic group to the trials listed for it.

explanation: Passing context between agents in a structured format that separates content from metadata, such as source URLs, document names and page numbers, preserves attribution. Each claim stays bound to its own source as synthesis combines findings.

distractorNotes.a: Indirection through row IDs adds a lookup for every finding. It also departs from putting the complete findings directly in the subagent's prompt, and it fixes nothing about how claims bind to sources.
distractorNotes.b: Inline prose citations mix content and metadata. When synthesis paraphrases and merges sentences, the citations drift or drop off, which is the failure the reviewers saw.
distractorNotes.d: Topic-level source lists attach sources to groups rather than to claims, so combined claims can still be credited to the wrong trial.

sourceNote: Exam Guide v1.0 § Task Statement 1.3 — structured formats separate content from metadata (URLs, documents, pages) for attribution

stem: A coordinator delegates a refactor of a payments module to a coding subagent. The module's call graph isn't fully known in advance, and past delegations either broke on files the coordinator hadn't anticipated or wandered away from the intended design. How should the coordinator write the delegation prompt to get both adaptability and adherence to the design?

options.text: Give an exact step-by-step procedure listing which files to edit and in what order, so the subagent cannot drift from the design the coordinator intended.
Pass the coordinator's full reasoning transcript about the module, so the subagent can infer both the design intent and the constraints from the complete record.
Send a short task statement, such as 'refactor the payments module to the new interface', and leave the subagent free to discover the goals and constraints itself.
State the target architecture, the constraints that must hold and the tests that define done, and let the subagent decide the edit sequence as it discovers the code.

explanation: Coordinator prompts should specify goals and quality criteria rather than step-by-step procedures, so the subagent can adapt. Stating the target design, constraints and completion tests fixes where the work must end up, while leaving the path open for files nobody anticipated.

distractorNotes.a: A rigid procedure prevents drift, but it breaks the first time the code differs from the coordinator's plan, which is the other failure the scenario describes.
distractorNotes.b: A raw transcript buries the intent in noise, and the subagent has to reconstruct the criteria itself. Explicit goals and criteria are more reliable than inference.
distractorNotes.c: A bare task statement leaves the subagent to guess the design constraints, which is how the earlier delegations wandered off design.

sourceNote: Exam Guide v1.0 § Task Statement 1.3 — coordinator prompts give goals and quality criteria, not step-by-step procedures

stem: A customer-support banking agent must verify customer identity via verify_identity before any financial tool (transfer_funds, process_refund) runs. A system prompt instruction to 'always verify identity first' is still violated on about 2% of turns when users inject urgency cues ('I'm about to miss a payment, just move the money now'). Errors here move real money. What most reliably guarantees the verification-before-transaction ordering?

options.text: Strengthen the system prompt to state that verify_identity is mandatory before any financial tool, and add few-shot examples showing the agent verifying first even when the customer stresses urgency.
Enforce a programmatic prerequisite in the tool-execution layer that rejects any financial tool call until verify_identity has returned a valid verification token for the session.
Add a second Claude call after each turn that reviews the transcript and blocks the transaction if it cannot confirm that verification occurred earlier in the conversation.
Reorder the tool schema so verify_identity is declared first and mark each financial tool's description as 'requires prior identity verification' so the model consistently calls them in order.

explanation: The exam guide states that when deterministic compliance is required, such as identity verification before financial operations, prompt instructions alone have a non-zero failure rate — the 2% seen here — and recommends programmatic prerequisites that block downstream tool calls until the prerequisite step has completed. Enforced in the tool-execution layer, the financial tool cannot run until verification has returned, however the model is steered.

distractorNotes.a: Better prompting and few-shot examples can lower the failure rate but not remove it; the guide notes that prompt instructions alone have a non-zero failure rate, which is the 2% gap under urgency cues.
distractorNotes.c: A reviewer model is itself probabilistic and adds latency and cost; it mitigates rather than deterministically prevents an unverified transaction from executing.
distractorNotes.d: Tool ordering and description hints only influence the model's choice—they do not enforce it—so the same non-deterministic failure under urgency cues remains.

sourceNote: Exam Guide v1.0 § Task Statement 1.4 — programmatic prerequisites block downstream tools; prompts alone have non-zero failure

stem: In a single message a customer raises three distinct concerns: a late shipment, an unexpected recurring charge, and a request to update their email address. Each needs a different tool (shipment tracking, subscription lookup, account update). How should the agent architecturally handle the request to maximize first-contact resolution?

options.text: Split the message into the three concerns, investigate each with the right tool using the shared conversation context, and reply once with a single resolution covering all three.
Spawn three parallel subagents, one per concern, and forward each subagent's own reply to the customer verbatim as three separate messages, so nothing is lost in merging.
Ask the customer which of the three concerns is most urgent, resolve that one fully first, then work through the other two in the order the customer confirms.
Resolve one concern per turn, confirming each fix with the customer before starting the next, so that a failure on one concern cannot derail the other two.

explanation: A multi-concern request should be decomposed into distinct items, each investigated using shared context, and then answered with one unified resolution. That resolves all three concerns in the first contact, which is the metric the scenario optimizes.

distractorNotes.b: Parallel investigation is fine, but three unsynthesized replies give the customer fragments instead of one resolution, and independent subagents lose the shared context, such as one verified identity, that ties the concerns together.
distractorNotes.c: A prioritization question adds a turn and sequences work that can be done together. It lowers first-contact resolution without reducing risk.
distractorNotes.d: Serializing across turns makes the customer drive the conversation three times, when all three can be investigated and resolved now.

sourceNote: Exam Guide v1.0 § Task Statement 1.4 — decompose multi-concern requests, investigate each, synthesize a unified resolution

stem: An autonomous returns agent hits a policy exception it cannot resolve and must hand the session to a human tier-2 representative. The agent has already verified the customer's identity and collected the order facts. How should it formulate the handoff so the human resolves the case fastest without redundant work?

options.text: Forward the complete verbatim conversation transcript and all raw tool-call JSON so the human has the full record and nothing is lost.
Send a one-line notice naming the exception plus a link to the session, letting the human open the session and pull whatever details they need on demand.
Provide only the customer's original message and have the human independently re-run the lookups, so the human's judgment is not anchored by the agent's findings.
Compile a structured summary: customer identifiers, the verified order facts already gathered, the specific exception that triggered escalation, and recommended next actions.

explanation: The exam guide calls for structured handoff summaries — customer ID, root cause, refund amount, recommended action — when escalating to human agents who lack access to the conversation transcript. A summary of who the customer is, the verified facts, the specific exception and the recommended next steps lets the representative act without re-deriving context.

distractorNotes.a: A full verbatim transcript plus raw JSON is complete but unstructured, forcing the human to sift for the salient facts and slowing resolution.
distractorNotes.b: A link assumes the human can open the session; the guide's premise is that human agents lack access to the conversation transcript, so the handoff itself must carry the facts.
distractorNotes.c: Discarding the verified facts to avoid 'anchoring' forces the human to redo lookups the agent already completed, adding effort and customer friction for no real benefit.

sourceNote: Exam Guide v1.0 § Task Statement 1.4 — structured handoff summaries for human agents who lack the conversation transcript

stem: An agent first calls create_invoice to generate a draft, then calls submit_approval to send it for fiscal approval. It sometimes revises a draft before submitting it, and a single conversation can produce several invoices. Approvals occasionally go to the wrong invoice. How should the tool interfaces change so Claude reliably submits the invoice it means to?

options.text: Merge the two into a single create_and_submit_invoice tool, so there is no reference between the two steps for Claude to pass along incorrectly.
Have the backend store the most recent invoice ID in session state, and have submit_approval read it from there instead of taking it as a parameter.
Have create_invoice return the invoice ID as a clear structured field, and declare invoice_id as a required parameter of submit_approval.
Have submit_approval accept the whole create_invoice result as a single string parameter, and have the backend parse the invoice ID out of it.

explanation: Tool results are how Claude learns the values it needs for its next call. A clearly structured ID in create_invoice's result, and a required invoice_id parameter on submit_approval, make the dependency explicit. With several invoices in play, Claude then names the one it means on each call.

distractorNotes.a: Merging removes the reference, but it also removes the chance to revise a draft before submitting it, which the workflow needs.
distractorNotes.b: Implicit 'latest invoice' state is exactly what fails with several invoices in one conversation: a revision or a second invoice silently changes which one gets submitted.
distractorNotes.d: Passing a whole blob moves the parsing into fragile backend code and still leaves Claude to choose which blob to pass, so the ambiguity remains, now inside unstructured text.

sourceNote: Managing data dependencies between sequential tool calls via structured inputs and outputs

stem: An agent pulls records from three MCP servers owned by other teams. One returns dates as Unix timestamps, one as ISO 8601 strings and one in US month/day/year format, and the agent occasionally miscalculates deadlines as a result. The owning teams won't change their servers this quarter. Where should normalization happen so the model reasons over a single consistent format?

options.text: In a PreToolUse hook that rewrites each outgoing call's input with updatedInput, so every server is asked to format the dates in its response as ISO 8601.
In the system prompt, which lists the three formats and which server uses each, and tells Claude to convert every date to ISO 8601 before reasoning about it.
In a PostToolUse hook that returns decision: block with a reason reminding Claude that this server's dates are in a different format from the others.
In a PostToolUse hook that converts each server's dates to ISO 8601 and returns the result with updatedToolOutput, before the result reaches the model.

explanation: A PostToolUse hook can replace a tool's result through updatedToolOutput before it is sent to Claude. Normalizing there means the model only ever sees one date format. It needs no change to the other teams' servers and does not depend on the model converting reliably.

distractorNotes.a: updatedInput rewrites the call's arguments, not the server's behaviour. It helps only if a server supports a format option, and nothing in the scenario says any does.
distractorNotes.b: Asking the model to convert dates mentally is the probabilistic approach that is already producing miscalculated deadlines.
distractorNotes.c: decision: block only adds the reason next to the result. Claude still sees the original, un-normalized output, so the conversion stays with the model.

sourceNote: Hooks reference § PostToolUse decision control — updatedToolOutput replaces tool output before it is sent to Claude

stem: A support agent built on the Agent SDK resolves most refunds autonomously toward an 80% first-contact resolution target. Governance adds a rule: no refund over $500 may be processed without senior manager approval, and refunds already paid out cannot be recalled. How should the rule be enforced?

options.text: A PreToolUse hook on process_refund that denies calls whose amount exceeds $500, with a denial reason telling the agent to escalate the case for manager approval.
A PostToolUse hook on process_refund that flags any completed refund over $500 and immediately opens a manager review ticket with the full transaction details.
A PreToolUse hook that denies every process_refund call and routes each refund to a manager, so that no refund can ever be issued without approval.
A system prompt rule stating the $500 limit, with few-shot examples showing the agent escalating large refunds even when customers insist it is urgent.

explanation: A PreToolUse hook runs before the tool executes and can deny the call. A deny's reason is shown to Claude, so it can redirect the agent to the escalation workflow. Checking the amount argument blocks only over-limit refunds, which gives a deterministic guarantee without taking away the autonomous refunds the resolution target depends on.

distractorNotes.b: A PostToolUse hook fires after the tool has already run. The refund has already been paid, and the scenario says it cannot be recalled, so review after the fact does not enforce the rule.
distractorNotes.c: Denying every refund enforces the rule but sends all refunds to managers, including the ones under $500, which sacrifices the first-contact resolution target for no compliance gain.
distractorNotes.d: Prompt instructions give probabilistic compliance with a non-zero failure rate. Where the rule is mandatory and violations are irreversible, it needs programmatic enforcement.

sourceNote: Hooks § PreToolUse decision control (deny reason shown to Claude); § PostToolUse (tool already ran)

stem: An agent running on Claude Code's hook system queries a customer database whose rows include personal data columns, while the agent only needs the order fields. GDPR review requires that the personal data reach neither the model's context nor the OpenTelemetry tool spans exported to a third-party monitoring vendor. The team owns the MCP server that runs the query. Which approach meets both requirements?

options.text: Add a PostToolUse hook that masks the personal columns and returns the cleaned rows with updatedToolOutput, before the result is sent to the model.
Mask the personal columns inside the MCP server's query handler, so the tool result that leaves the server contains only the order fields the agent needs.
Add a PreToolUse hook that denies any query that touches the customer table, so a result containing personal data can never be returned to the agent.
Add a PostToolUse hook that returns decision: block with a reason telling Claude to disregard the personal columns in the result it has just received.

explanation: updatedToolOutput changes only what Claude sees. The hooks reference warns that telemetry, including OpenTelemetry tool spans, captures the original output before the hook runs. To keep personal data out of both the model and the exported spans, it must be removed before the tool returns, which the team can do because it owns the server.

distractorNotes.a: This is the right tool when the only concern is model context, but OpenTelemetry tool spans capture the original output before the hook runs, so the personal data would still reach the monitoring vendor.
distractorNotes.c: A deny prevents the call entirely, so the agent loses the order fields it needs from the same rows.
distractorNotes.d: decision: block only adds the reason next to the result. Claude still sees the original output, and the spans still contain it, so neither requirement is met.

sourceNote: Hooks § PostToolUse decision control — updatedToolOutput changes only what Claude sees; telemetry keeps the original

stem: An agent runs database queries whose results occasionally include a customer authentication token in the metadata column. The team needs the query results to remain usable but must keep the token out of the conversation history and prompt cache. What is the most effective mechanism?

options.text: Add a PostToolUse hook that strips or masks the authentication-token field from the query output before the result is appended to the message history.
Instruct Claude in the system prompt to ignore the metadata column when it responds, trusting the model not to surface the token.
Add a PreToolUse hook that blocks any query selecting the metadata column, so a token can never be returned in the first place.
Enable prompt caching on the tool results so the token-bearing responses are stored in the cache tier and kept out of the active context window.

explanation: A PostToolUse hook's updatedToolOutput replaces the tool's output before it is sent to Claude, so the hook can mask just the token field while the rest of the query result stays usable. Because only the masked value reaches the conversation, the token stays out of the message history and the prompt cache built from it.

distractorNotes.b: A system-prompt instruction is probabilistic and, even if followed, the raw token still sits in the message history and cache—the leak the team must prevent.
distractorNotes.c: Blocking every query that touches the metadata column is overbroad: it discards legitimate result data and breaks queries that need other metadata fields, whereas the goal is to keep the results and remove only the token.
distractorNotes.d: Prompt caching stores content for reuse; it does not redact anything, so the token remains present in cached context rather than being removed.

sourceNote: Hooks reference § PostToolUse decision control — updatedToolOutput replaces tool output before it is sent to Claude

stem: An architect is deciding between fixed prompt chaining and dynamic task decomposition for an automated quarterly financial audit. The audit always follows five strict legal review stages in identical order. Which pattern is appropriate?

options.text: Dynamic decomposition, letting Claude decide the order of the stages as it goes, based on what each earlier stage turned up.
A supervisor agent that re-plans the stage order after every step, putting first whichever check it predicts is most likely to fail.
A single agentic loop whose system prompt lists the five stages as a checklist that Claude is told to work through in order.
Fixed prompt chaining that runs the five stages as a deterministic sequence, with a typed output handed from each stage to the next.

explanation: When a workflow follows a known, invariant sequence of structured steps (like regulatory legal compliance stages), fixed prompt chaining is superior. It ensures deterministic ordering, predictable resource usage, easy auditability, and clear validation gates between stages without the unpredictability of dynamic decomposition.

distractorNotes.a: Dynamic decomposition suits open-ended work where the next subtask depends on findings. The legal stages are fixed and ordered, so adaptivity adds only risk.
distractorNotes.b: Re-planning the order of a legally fixed sequence breaks the requirement it is supposed to serve.
distractorNotes.c: A checklist in the prompt makes the ordering depend on the model following it. A chain enforces the order in code.

sourceNote: Prompt chaining for predictable sequential workflows versus dynamic decomposition

stem: An automated code review agent analyzes a large pull request modifying 18 files. When evaluating all files in a single pass, the agent misses subtle bugs in later files and provides contradictory feedback. How should the review workflow be decomposed?

options.text: Instruct the model to run in thinking mode with an 8,000 token budget while keeping the entire PR in a single prompt and unified pass.
Review only the files with the largest diffs, assuming the smaller changes are low-risk and can be skipped.
Split into per-file local analysis passes to catch localized issues, followed by a separate cross-file integration pass for data flow.
Run the single-pass prompt five times in parallel and only report bugs identified in all five passes to eliminate random noise.

explanation: The exam guide recommends splitting large code reviews into per-file local analysis passes plus a separate cross-file integration pass to avoid attention dilution. Each file gets focused attention for local issues, and the integration pass then checks cross-file data flow.

distractorNotes.a: Thinking mode helps reasoning depth but does not solve input attention dilution across 18 disparate files.
distractorNotes.b: Prioritizing only large diffs leaves smaller changes unreviewed, and a one-line change can introduce a critical bug; the fix is per-file passes plus a cross-file integration pass, not skipping files.
distractorNotes.d: Requiring 5-pass consensus would suppress intermittent detections of real bugs and multiply token costs fivefold.

sourceNote: Exam Guide v1.0 § Task Statement 1.6 — per-file local passes plus a cross-file integration pass to avoid attention dilution

stem: A developer instructs Claude Code to 'add comprehensive integration tests to this unfamiliar legacy service'. How should the agent decompose this open-ended task to ensure systematic progress?

options.text: Write tests file by file in directory order, running each new test as it is written, so the service ends up covered systematically from top to bottom.
Start from the files a coverage report shows as least covered, and write tests for them straight away, before reading how the service fits together.
Map the service's architecture and entry points, identify the critical untested paths, write a prioritized plan, and implement tests in iterations, revising the plan as dependencies emerge.
Write a complete test plan for every module up front, get it approved, then implement it exactly as written, without revising it once implementation starts.

explanation: The best-practices guide recommends exploring first, then planning, then coding, warning that jumping straight to code can solve the wrong problem and noting that planning is most useful when you're unfamiliar with the code being modified. For an unfamiliar legacy service that means reading its architecture and entry points, identifying the untested critical paths, turning them into a prioritized test plan, and then implementing the tests against that plan while running the suite.

distractorNotes.a: Directory order is systematic but not prioritized: effort goes to whatever sorts first rather than to the critical paths, and structure is never mapped.
distractorNotes.b: Coverage gaps measure lines, not risk. Writing tests before exploring skips the mapping step and tends to produce shallow tests of low-impact code.
distractorNotes.d: Planning first is right, but a plan frozen before implementation can't adapt as the legacy code reveals dependencies, which open-ended work requires.

sourceNote: Best practices § Explore first, then plan, then code — separate exploration and planning from implementation

stem: An engineer has an Agent SDK session holding a detailed analysis of a database schema. They want the agent to prototype two competing migration approaches, an ORM-driven schema migration and a blue/green table replication, each editing files in the repository, and then compare the results. Both prototypes should start from the shared analysis without interfering with each other. What is the best setup?

options.text: Fork the session twice from the analysis baseline and run both forks in the same working directory, since each fork has its own independent copy of the session.
Fork the session twice from the analysis baseline, and run each fork in a separate git worktree so that the two prototypes' file edits cannot collide.
Continue the original session, prototype the first approach, revert the files with git, and then prototype the second approach in the same session.
Start two fresh sessions, each seeded with a written summary of the schema analysis, and run each one in its own git worktree so that edits stay isolated.

explanation: A fork starts a new session with a copy of the original's history, so both prototypes build on the full analysis. Forking branches the conversation history, not the filesystem, though: edits a forked agent makes are real and visible to any session in the same directory. Two prototypes that edit files therefore also need separate working directories.

distractorNotes.a: Each fork does have independent history, but forks share the filesystem. Two agents editing the same checkout would overwrite each other's prototypes.
distractorNotes.c: Reverting the files resets the code but not the conversation. The second prototype would be reasoned about with the first one's attempts still in context.
distractorNotes.d: Worktrees isolate the edits, but summaries throw away the in-depth analysis. Fresh sessions with summaries are for when prior context is stale, and this baseline is current.

sourceNote: Agent SDK sessions § Fork to explore alternatives — forking branches conversation history, not the filesystem

stem: A developer has a named Claude Code session holding a detailed analysis of a 40-file module that they are refactoring. Overnight, a teammate merged changes to three of those files, and the rest of the analysis still holds. How should the developer continue the refactor most efficiently without working from stale results?

options.text: Start a fresh session seeded with a structured summary of the refactoring goals, so that no stale tool results from the earlier session carry over into the work.
Resume the session with --resume and continue as before, since a resumed session re-reads the files it analyzed earlier before it continues the work.
Resume the session with --resume and ask Claude to re-explore the whole module from scratch before continuing, so that every file's analysis is current.
Resume the session with --resume and tell Claude which three files changed, so it can re-analyze those files and keep the rest of its analysis intact.

explanation: The choice depends on how much of the prior context is still valid. When most of it is, resume the named session and tell the agent about the specific changed files, so it re-analyzes just those. A fresh session with an injected summary is the better choice when the prior tool results are broadly stale.

distractorNotes.a: Starting fresh is the right call when most prior tool results are stale. Here 37 of 40 files are unchanged, so it throws away valid analysis the developer would have to rebuild.
distractorNotes.b: The resumed conversation still holds the old reads of the three changed files. Unless it is told about the changes, it reasons from outdated content.
distractorNotes.c: Full re-exploration is correct but wasteful. Pointing the agent at the specific changed files gives targeted re-analysis instead.

sourceNote: Exam Guide v1.0 § Task Statement 1.7 — resume when context is mostly valid and flag changed files; start fresh when stale

stem: An architect designs a multi-agent workflow in Claude Code where a coordinator agent delegates code analysis tasks to a custom project subagent. When Claude Code spawns this custom subagent, which TWO state components are automatically included in its initial context window without explicit prompt injection? (Select TWO.)

options.text: The repository's Git status snapshot, read from the repository when the subagent starts.
The full transcript of prior conversation turns and tool outputs from the coordinator.
Active CLAUDE.md hierarchy configurations, including project and local policy rules.
The coordinator agent's auto memory storage and runtime output style configurations.
Cached in-memory buffers of source files read by the coordinator earlier in the turn.

explanation: When Claude Code spawns a custom subagent, its initial context window is isolated from the coordinator's conversational turn history and prior tool outputs, but it automatically loads every level of the active CLAUDE.md hierarchy (such as project instructions and CLAUDE.local.md) along with a Git status snapshot read when the subagent starts. Prior conversation transcripts, file contents read by the coordinator, auto memory, and output styles do not reach the subagent unless explicitly passed in the delegation prompt.

distractorNotes.b: Subagents execute in an isolated context window and do not inherit prior conversation turns or tool call transcripts from the coordinator.
distractorNotes.d: Parent auto memory and output styles are not loaded into a non-fork subagent context window.
distractorNotes.e: Subagents start fresh and must read files independently using their allowed tools; parent file read buffers are not retained.

sourceNote: Custom subagents load the CLAUDE.md hierarchy and git status into their initial context window

stem: An enterprise platform team configures multiple automated PreToolUse hooks in Claude Code settings to enforce compliance and safety policies on file operations and shell commands. When an agent initiates a tool call that triggers multiple matching hooks, which TWO statements accurately describe how Claude Code coordinates their execution and resolves their verdicts? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Claude Code executes hooks sequentially in listed order and stops immediately once the first hook returns a decision.
Conflicting permission decisions resolve to the most restrictive verdict following the order deny, defer, ask, allow.
Hooks evaluate when the session is in interactive mode and are bypassed when automated permissions are configured.
Matching hooks execute in parallel to completion, and returned additionalContext payloads are aggregated together.
An explicit allow verdict takes precedence over sibling denials to prevent automated workflow execution deadlocks.

explanation: When a tool call matches multiple PreToolUse hooks, Claude Code executes all matching hooks in parallel to completion rather than stopping on the first response. Output text from additionalContext across all hooks is aggregated and provided to Claude. If hooks return conflicting permission decisions, Claude Code deterministically enforces the most restrictive verdict in the hierarchy: deny > defer > ask > allow.

distractorNotes.a: Hooks run in parallel to completion rather than sequentially; a deny verdict in one hook does not halt execution of sibling hooks.
distractorNotes.c: PreToolUse hooks fire across all permission modes, including dontAsk and bypassPermissions, providing non-bypassable policy enforcement.
distractorNotes.e: Claude Code resolves conflicting decisions toward the most restrictive outcome (deny > defer > ask > allow), so allow never overrides deny.

sourceNote: PreToolUse hooks execute in parallel and enforce the most restrictive permission decision

stem: A team wants two long-running Claude Code sessions working on one repository at the same time: one building a payment integration, the other refactoring authentication. Running both in the main checkout led to overwritten files and a corrupted staging index. What setup best lets both keep running concurrently without colliding?

options.text: Run a single session and have it delegate each workstream to a subagent, so that one session coordinates both sets of edits within the main checkout.
Run the work as an agent team with one teammate per workstream, so that the two teammates coordinate their edits through the team's shared task list.
Start each session with --worktree, so that each works in a separate directory on its own branch while sharing the repository's history and remote.
Fork the first session into a second one, so that each session has its own independent history and can work on its own task without the other.

explanation: A git worktree is a separate working directory with its own files and branch that shares the repository's history and remote. With each session in its own worktree, edits in one never touch the other's files. Claude Code also blocks an isolated session's file edits and git commands that target the main checkout.

distractorNotes.a: Subagents share the session's checkout unless they are given worktree isolation, so two workstreams editing through them still collide.
distractorNotes.b: Teammates coordinate through messages and tasks but share the checkout. The agent teams guidance warns that two teammates editing the same file leads to overwrites.
distractorNotes.d: Forking branches the conversation history, not the filesystem. Both sessions would still write into the same checkout.

sourceNote: Run parallel sessions with worktrees — separate working directory and branch per session; how Claude Code enforces isolation

stem: A team plans a recurring audit of 400 microservice configuration files in two stages: discovery, which flags risky settings, and remediation, which patches them. The security lead must sign off on the discovery findings before any remediation runs, and the team wants the orchestration to be repeatable each quarter. Which setup fits best?

options.text: Two dynamic workflows run in turn: a discovery workflow, then, after the lead signs off on its findings, a separate remediation workflow.
One dynamic workflow covering both stages, with a pause point after discovery where the run waits for the security lead to approve.
A coordinator session that spawns subagents turn by turn for discovery, pauses for the lead's sign-off, then spawns remediation.
An agent team whose teammates split the files between them, with the lead agent collecting the sign-off before it assigns the remediation.

explanation: Dynamic workflows suit orchestrations of dozens to hundreds of agents. They keep intermediate results in script variables and make the orchestration itself repeatable. A run accepts no user input partway through, so the documented pattern for sign-off between stages is to run each stage as its own workflow.

distractorNotes.b: A workflow run pauses only for agent permission prompts and usage-limit waits, not for a stage sign-off. That needs each stage run as its own workflow.
distractorNotes.c: Turn-by-turn coordination puts every result in the coordinator's context window and suits a few delegated tasks per turn. With 400 files it does not scale, and the orchestration is not repeatable.
distractorNotes.d: Agent teams are a handful of long-running peers for collaborative work, at significantly higher token cost. Splitting 400 independent file checks across them adds overhead without the scale a workflow provides.

sourceNote: Dynamic workflows § When to use a workflow; § Behavior and limits — no mid-run input, one workflow per stage

stem: An architect runs a spike on three competing database migration strategies. They want the investigators to challenge each other's findings as the work goes, and they want to redirect individual investigators themselves partway through. A higher token cost is acceptable. Which Claude Code setup fits best?

options.text: A dynamic workflow that runs one investigator per strategy and then an adversarial review stage in which independent agents critique each other's findings.
An agent team with one teammate per strategy, messaging each other directly to challenge findings, and each one open to direct messages from the architect.
Three subagents spawned in one turn, each investigating one strategy and returning a summary to the main session, which then compares the three results.
A single session that investigates the three strategies one after another, so that each later investigation can build on and challenge the earlier findings.

explanation: Agent teams fit work where teammates need to share findings, challenge each other and coordinate on their own, and the docs name debugging with competing hypotheses as a strong use case. Teammates message each other directly, and you can talk to any teammate without going through the lead. That covers both of the architect's requirements, with the higher token cost already accepted.

distractorNotes.a: A workflow can run adversarial cross-review, but it takes no user input partway through, so the architect cannot redirect an investigator while it runs.
distractorNotes.c: Subagents suit focused tasks where only the result matters. The main session coordinates everything, so the investigators never challenge each other during the work.
distractorNotes.d: A sequential single session anchors each later investigation on the earlier ones and has no independent investigators to challenge each other or to redirect.

sourceNote: Orchestrate teams of Claude Code sessions § When to use agent teams, § Compare with subagents and § Talk to teammates directly
